s16.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — ELEVEN COATS

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Tuesday at the Anchor he pitched me New Orleans on the placemats — the game at the Broussards’, a week, Bacchus — with six tickets printed and paid for, one with my name on it. Then he said he’s never asked me for anything, and he was asking. I said no. He folded the placemat in thirds and said it’s refundable. Thursday night he packed eleven coats for a warm city and left me a DVD for every night he’s gone. In the dark he asked, answer to what. I told him Nonna’s question, her words: *Quale ti fa pregare.*

body: Eleven coats lie across Theo’s bed with their sleeves arranged, shoulder to shoulder, a lineup in which no one is the suspect. Jack counts them from the doorway with the toothbrush still in his mouth. It comes out eleven.

On the windowsill the speaker is playing strings, something French and sad and expensive. The casement is open an inch on the dark and the eucalyptus, and Theo, in his shirtsleeves, is going down the row with a lint roller, a coat at a time, and doing the camel last, as if it might hear.

“Sixty-two degrees in New Orleans,” he says, “and every drop of humidity God ever made. Cashmere is out. Tweed would be a statement, and the statement would be *sweat*. I’m bringing the linen and the regret.”

body.text: Folding the linen, not looking up: “You could have just said no.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “She showed Laney your penmanship.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “That one was beneath you, Costigan.”
Folding the linen, not looking up: “She’s waiting for an answer, you know.” “She has one.”

body: Jack sits on the edge of his own bed. His half of 412 is a footlocker, a crucifix and a hook with a Carhartt on it, and he has nothing whatever to pack. On the closet door, across the room, a black Saints jersey hangs on a hanger, number 9, with the tags still on and a pocket square folded into the collar. “For the city,” Theo says, catching him looking. “A guest brings something.”
On the desk stands a stack of DVD cases, and every case has a yellow Post-it on its spine, in fountain pen. FRI. SAT. SUN — AFTER THE GAME. MON. The days go on up the pile to SUN 14.
“One for every night I’m gone,” Theo says, without turning around. “For a man who’s staying.”

Jack takes the top one. *The Third Man.* “A zither,” Theo says. “You’ll hate it by the end of the first reel and miss it by Monday. Wait for the last shot. A cemetery road, some trees, a woman. No one says a word. It’s the best thing anyone ever did with a road.” Under it, *Rififi*: “Half an hour of four men robbing a jeweler without a word of dialogue. You’ll find it restful.” Under that, SUN — AFTER THE GAME, *It’s a Wonderful Life*, and Jack looks up.
“For the loser,” Theo says. “Whoever it is. It works on both.”

Monday is *Paths of Glory*, and Jack says Monday looks grim. “Monday is Monday. I’m not a monster, Costigan. Go to the bottom.” The bottom is the fourteenth, *The Apartment*. “A man strains spaghetti through a tennis racket and a woman plays gin. You’ll be fine.”
“Skye leaves Saturday at six,” Jack says. “Sixteen days.”

“Then you’re a man alone in a dormitory with a laptop and a stack of films,” Theo says. “I’m told that’s how monasteries get started.” He holds a coat up to the light, finds nothing wrong with it, and hangs it. “Pruitt will find you by Sunday. He has the instincts of a dowser.”
“Theo.” Jack says it to the Post-its. “About Tuesday.”
“Tuesday was a pitch. Pitches die. It’s what they’re for.” Theo rolls the camel’s lapel and smooths it flat. “I’d apologize, but I already owe you a kidney, and I won’t be put into arrears.
“You don’t owe me a kidney.”

“I owe everyone a kidney, Costigan. It’s how I stay solvent.” He tips his head at the desk. “The MacBook stays. It has the drive. You may use it. You may even ask. The password is *hollis*, lowercase, and if Priya ever learns it I will know where she got it.”
“I’ll ask.”

“I’ll know if you don’t.” He crosses to the mirror, where Nonna’s twenty is still tucked in the frame where he put it at Thanksgiving, and takes it out, and turns it over to the back, and tucks it in again. The iPhone is propped against a sleeve on the bedspread, and he reads the weather off it to the room. “Sixty-two, clear through Sunday. The Saints are getting the sun.” The little screen slides sideways under his finger to the next city. “My mother’s under the burn. They’re saying rain Friday.”
“Tell her hello.”
“She’ll ask if you’re eating,” Theo says. “They always ask.”

He zips ten of the coats into the long bag and leaves the camel over the desk chair for the morning, and moves Hollis from the nightstand to the sill beside the speaker. Jack hits the overhead on his way to bed. The streetlight lays the blind across the ceiling in stripes, and the strings come round to their theme again.
“There’s still a seat,” Theo says, from the dark.
“Goodnight, Theo.”
“Goodnight, Father Jack.”

body.text: “Last week I asked if she’s the answer and you said *Yeah. It is.*” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”
“You’ve told me twice she’s the answer.” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”
“You keep saying *the answer* like it’s on a plaque.” A pause from the other bed. “Answer to what, Costigan?”

choices.text: Tell him the question. All of it.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna’s question, all of it, in her words, for the first time in your life: *Due ragazze. Quale ti fa pregare.*
response: Jack says it to the ceiling. It comes out in his grandmother’s accent, the only one he has for it, and he had not known it would come at all: Christmas night, the phone lit in his hand, her beads going. “*Due ragazze.* Two girls. *Quale ti fa pregare.* Which one makes you pray.”
The blind stripes lie on the ceiling and do nothing. When Theo speaks it is very low. “*Which* one.”
Theo turns over to face the wall. He says nothing else, and the strings go on a long time without anybody.

choices.text: Tell him, and then tell him the answer.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna’s question — which one makes you pray — and then the answer: she does.
response: “*Quale ti fa pregare.*” It is the first time he has said it aloud, and it comes out in Nonna’s accent, the way she said it on Christmas night over her beads. “Which one makes you pray. It’s what she asked me. And she does.”
“You did.” The speaker, still on, clicks off at the end of the record.

choices.text: “Pasta, Theo. She asked about pasta.” Then the real one.
choices.key: In the dark Theo asked, answer to what. You told him Nonna asked about pasta. Then you told him the real question: which one makes you pray.
response: So Jack gives him the real one, in Italian and then in English, and it is the first time in his life he has said either aloud: *Quale ti fa pregare.* Which one makes you pray.
That gets no answer. Outside the window the eucalyptus goes in a south wind that has brought nothing yet.

s17.slug: FRIDAY · 10:15 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE CURB — THE CAR SERVICE

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Tuesday at the Fishbowl she passed me the popcorn and then remembered not to. Wednesday they were all in 412 when I came back for my jacket: her birthday, she said — the fourteenth; she’ll be in New Orleans. Friday at the curb: “Have a nice weekend, fireman.”

journal.title: New Orleans
journal.text: The Saints are in the Super Bowl. Friday morning Theo, Lena, Laney, Kevin and Margot left for New Orleans in a black car with a driver Theo’s known since the seventh grade: the game at the Broussards’, then a week, then Bacchus. Home the fifteenth. Six tickets; one had my name on it. Theo says he’ll hold my seat. I told him don’t. Sunday I’m on Doug’s futon with Yusuf.

body: The fog burned off by nine and left a high white sky, and the wind has gone around to the south, warm, with dust in it. Every palm on the Delgado lawn leans toward the 101. At the curb a black Lincoln Navigator has taken the whole red zone with its hazards going, and beside its open tailgate stands a man in a gray overcoat who has plainly been waiting for Theo Vance since the seventh grade.

On the top step Priya Raman has appeared in her RA lanyard with a stopwatch and a laminated card. “Per the Residential Life Handbook,” she tells the driver, “a vehicle in the red zone has five minutes.”
“Miss,” says the man in the overcoat, “I am a professional.”
“So is the handbook.” She starts the watch.

“Arturo,” Theo announces, coming down the steps with the camel coat over his arm, and says it to Jack as though introducing a cathedral. “Arturo drove me to my First Communion and my first arrest, Costigan. Both were misunderstandings.”
“Mr. Costigan,” Arturo says, and takes the garment bag out of Theo’s other hand before it can be explained.

Jack stops on the third step down from the doors and goes no farther. He has come down because staying upstairs would have been its own kind of message, and he has no message. The loading is a negotiation. Laney’s four bags go in largest first under Arturo’s direction (“Arturo, darlin’, that one rides with me. It has my *face* in it”), and her garment bag is carried down by Laney herself and laid on top like a patient. Margot’s one black duffel goes in last and takes up less room than Laney’s hat. Kevin’s roller bag has a tag on the handle in his mother’s marker: KEVIN TRAN — CALL MA WHEN YOU LAND. Theo casts the seats like a picture: Laney by the window, Margot behind the driver, Kevin on the curb side so he can get out first and check everything.
Margot shakes Jack’s hand once, like a colleague’s. “I’m told it’s a matriarchy disguised as a parade,” she says. “I’ll be taking notes.”

Kevin goes in for the handshake and gives it up halfway, and it becomes a hug with the handshake still caught in the middle. “Disclosure,” he says, into the shoulder of the Carhartt. “This is a hug. I’m not charting it.”

Laney comes down the steps in a gold scarf she has bought for the cameras and walks straight up to Jack, and her hands go to the collar of the Carhartt where it’s folding under and flatten it. “Have a nice weekend, fireman,” she says, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, smiling with every tooth. She looks at her own hands. The sunglasses come down, and she goes to the car, and in the second row of the Navigator she is a pair of black lenses behind tinted glass, pointed at the steps. Jack stands with the collar flat where she left it.

Lena comes down the steps last, with her duffel over her shoulder and the pie box in both hands. She passes him on the step close enough that the corner of the box nearly brushes his sleeve. She doesn’t say anything, and he doesn’t. Arturo takes the duffel, and the box, and she gets in on the far side.
On the bench by the bike rack Yusuf Noorzai has been reading *Nine Stories* since before the Lincoln came, and has not turned a page. He turns one now.
At the car door Kevin counts off the party on one finger, as he counts everything. “Five,” he says. “That’s correct.” The smile comes up a little late.

Theo is the only one still talking. “Pecan,” he says, to the curb in general. “I told Gloria on Tuesday. She boxed one for the grandmother. Gloria has views on matriarchs.” He stands at the open door with the camel coat, and then he stops talking. “I’ll hold your seat.”
“Don’t.”
“I’ll hold it anyway.”

In the third row the far seat is empty. Theo lays the camel coat across it, collar up, and brings the belt over the coat and clicks it home. Then he gets in beside Margot, and Arturo shuts the doors one at a time, and the Navigator goes down the drive.
At the stop sign at the end of the drive the Lincoln’s brake lights come on and stay on a little longer than the sign needs, and then it turns toward the 101.
Priya clicks the stopwatch. “Four-forty,” she announces, and writes it on the card, and goes in.
The RAZR goes off in the pocket of the Carhartt, three times in a minute, and Jack reads them standing on the step in the wind from the south.

body: Behind him the door opens, and Doug comes out onto the top step in a Tauren druid T-shirt and his socks, holding a bowl of Froot Loops against his chest like a baby. “Dude,” he says. “Super Bowl. My futon. Yusuf’s in.”

response: “Duuuude,” says Doug, over five vowels. He goes back in to tell the futon.
Doug takes the nod as a blood oath. “Bring chips,” he calls up the stairwell after him. “Not the healthy ones.”
